target: AG1’s claim that AI benefits in everyday life, health, work, education, accessibility, and safety outweigh harms.
objection: AI commonly requires collecting and inferring from sensitive personal data, which creates ongoing privacy risks; it can also perpetuate racial bias from training data, displace labor and harm businesses through automation, and reduce students’ and adults’ independent critical thinking through over-reliance.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy, bias, labor, and learning harms are unavoidable in AI deployments.
objection: Organizations can use privacy-preserving controls, encryption, anonymization, auditing, human-in-the-loop oversight, worker reskilling, and education designs that require active practice, so the harms are not inevitable and can be materially reduced.

target: AG1’s claim that safeguards can reliably reduce privacy and discrimination harms.
objection: Even with encryption, anonymization, and monitoring, AI can still leak sensitive attributes through inference and can still produce biased outputs as data and use-cases shift, while economic and learning harms can persist despite attempted transition planning.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s harms reliably outweigh its benefits in practice.
objection: With integrated governance—privacy-preserving handling, continuous fairness monitoring, human oversight, worker transition support, and education designs that preserve active practice—real deployments can prevent or substantially block the major harms, so the harms do not necessarily outweigh the benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that safeguards can prevent the combined privacy, discrimination, economic, and learning harms across real deployments.
objection: The same large-scale deployment features that create privacy leakage and discrimination also tend to create economic displacement and reduced independent practice, so the proposed safeguards do not reliably eliminate the harms in real-world use.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy, discrimination, economic, and learning harms are recurring properties of AI deployments.
objection: Many beneficial AI applications can be designed with limited or local data processing so they do not inherently infer sensitive attributes, and AI can also be built to preserve or improve learning, reduce workplace injury, and raise productivity and economic well-being.

target: AG2’s claim that AI accessibility tools still inherently carry the same privacy/discrimination harms.
objection: Accessibility tools like speech-to-text, captions, and image descriptions often just transform the user’s own input into assistive output and do not require ongoing sensitive-attribute inference for downstream decisions, so those harms are not inherent to these uses.

target: AG2’s claim that healthcare AI necessarily weakens the benefits case because of harm mechanisms.
objection: In healthcare, AI can operate as decision support under clinician accountability and oversight, improving monitoring, risk detection, and care coordination; thus the claimed harm mechanism is substantially weakened in clinician-supervised deployments.

target: AG1’s claim that clinician oversight meaningfully prevents harmful healthcare AI outcomes.
objection: In practice, clinicians often receive AI recommendations inside busy workflows and can over-rely on them due to automation bias, making independent review often inadequate or effectively ignored.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be good for society if it improves accountability, recourse, and mitigation.
objection: A technology is not good for society if it systematically undermines people’s ability to understand and challenge consequential decisions, and many AI systems are opaque black boxes that are hard to inspect or contest, which harms minorities, privacy, and critical thinking.

target: AG2’s claim that opacity makes meaningful contestability impossible.
objection: AI can be deployed with accountable human decision-makers, practical explanations, documentation, and appeal channels, so affected people can still have meaningful contestability even if the model itself is complex or partially opaque.

target: AG1’s claim that documentation and human oversight provide meaningful contestability.
objection: Meaningful contestability requires causally faithful reasons and recourse that can actually change the outcome; generic explanations or discretionary human review do not satisfy that standard when they are only post-hoc or non-binding.

target: AG2’s claim that governance explanations are merely post-hoc and not causally faithful.
objection: If an explanation is generated from the same decision computation and exact inputs/features used for the output, it can be causally faithful, and appeal processes can genuinely correct outcomes when they re-check those decision factors.

target: AG1’s claim that contestability is practically accessible at scale.
objection: Meaningful contestability must be realistically accessible within operational timelines and at feasible personal cost, but individualized explanations and human appeals are labor-intensive and do not scale well for high-volume consequential decisions such as screening, eligibility, pricing, and hiring triage.

target: AG2’s claim that scaling makes contestability infeasible.
objection: Contestability does not require individualized human explanation in every case; scalable standardized explanations, streamlined appeals, and independent auditing can make recourse practically accessible even in high-volume deployments.

target: AG1’s claim that scalable contestability mechanisms are feasible.
objection: In high-volume consequential AI settings, real contestability still needs causally faithful explanations and effective outcome-correction, which requires substantial human labor, expertise, and fast turnaround that typical organizations cannot provide at scale.

target: AG2’s claim that high-volume AI inevitably makes contestability unavailable.
objection: Standardized decision-relevant explanations, logs, streamlined appeals, and independent oversight can provide practical contestability at scale, so high-volume AI does not inherently make recourse unavailable.

target: AG1’s claim that standardized explanations and logs are enough for meaningful contestability.
objection: Meaningful contestability requires individualized, decision-relevant reasons; generic explanations and logs are insufficient, and providing the needed individualized reasons would usually require revealing or reconstructing the sensitive inferences that drove the decision.

target: AG2’s claim that individualized contestability disclosures necessarily create dangerous privacy risks.
objection: Contestability can be provided through privacy-minimized, decision-relevant explanations, and privacy-preserving techniques like encryption, data minimization, and differential-privacy-style methods can bound leakage, so individualized disclosures need not create dangerous privacy harms.
